Constraint Handling Rules (CHR) is a declarative, logic-based language designed for constraint solving. It has gained significant traction in logic programming, particularly within Prolog, due to its simplicity and efficiency. This paper examines the expressive power of multiple heads in CHR by analyzing how constraints can be encoded using a restricted variant featuring only a single head. We demonstrate that CHR with multiple heads possesses greater expressive power than a standard version limited to a single head. Specifically, we identify a class of single-head constraints that, when combined with a finite set of rule definitions, enable encoding of any CHR program with a finite set of rules. This result is significant because it allows the encoding of general CHR programs with multiple heads into a restricted single-head variant.

We investigated the potential asymmetry in the spin directions of galaxies by analyzing the distribution of their projected rotation vectors. Our study utilized 10,000 galaxies from the Dark Energy Survey (DES), selected based on photometric redshifts and confirmed by spectroscopy, to determine the observed rotation direction. Our results indicate a slight excess of galaxies rotating in one projected direction, though this preference is not statistically significant. We further compared our findings with data from four other major sky surveys: SDSS, GAMA, 2dF, and GAMA. While the SDSS and GAMA surveys showed a marginally higher count of galaxies rotating in one direction, the 2dF survey exhibited a stronger preference for the opposite rotation direction.

Meta-learning has recently demonstrated significant success in few-shot learning, with the MAML algorithm being a prominent example. However, MAML's reliance on gradient-based optimization makes it susceptible to catastrophic forgetting, particularly in few-shot settings. This paper introduces Eigen-Reptile, a new meta-learning framework that integrates the advantages of Reptile with insights from eigen-learning. By employing Reptile's first-order update rule, Eigen-Reptile mitigates forgetting while maintaining rapid convergence. Additionally, it utilizes eigen-learning to enhance robustness against adversarial attacks and label noise. Experimental results on standard benchmarks, including the mini-Imagenet and CIFAR-100 datasets, confirm that Eigen-Reptile outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Notably, it achieves a 95.0% accuracy on the mini-Imagenet with 5-way 5-shot tasks and a 90.0% accuracy on the CIFAR-100 with 5-way 5-shot tasks, surpassing the performance of MAML.

We introduce a novel, interpretable framework designed to generate feature-level attributions for classification and regression tasks, specifically tailored for analyzing individual brain scans in neurological studies. This approach utilizes a gradient-based method to identify the spatial distribution of relevant brain regions, which are then condensed into a concise set of representative areas. These regions are subsequently visualized as a 3D brain map to illustrate the neurological signatures associated with specific conditions. To validate this method, we applied it to two distinct datasets: one involving automated classification of Alzheimer's disease versus normal controls, and another addressing regression of hippocampal volume in Alzheimer's patients. Results demonstrated that the model successfully identified known biomarkers linked to the respective tasks, thereby confirming its efficacy.

The growing prominence of AI ethics has led to a significant expansion of scholarly work in this domain. However, the field remains surprisingly immature, characterized by a lack of consensus on its fundamental nature, scope, and primary objectives. This article aims to advance the discourse on the state of AI ethics and identify future research trajectories. Specifically, the author argues that the field is overly fixated on the "narrow" or central concerns of AI ethics, which primarily involve the moral evaluation of algorithms and the development of ethical machine learning. In contrast, the author contends that the "margins" of AI ethics—encompassing the moral implications of data collection, the governance of data infrastructures, and the socio-economic consequences of AI deployment—deserve greater attention.

This study introduces a deep learning (DL) framework for cell-free massive MIMO (CF-mMIMO) systems that jointly estimates and forecasts channel states to mitigate channel aging. The proposed method alternates between estimating the current channel and predicting the next one, utilizing a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network to model temporal dependencies. By training the LSTM on data from a CF-mMIMO system, the approach learns to capture the underlying channel evolution patterns. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that this joint estimation and forecasting strategy significantly outperforms conventional channel estimation techniques that do not account for aging.

We examine the electromagnetic contributions to the decay rate of $ud \to \ell \nu_\ell$ in the framework of the Standard Model, incorporating recent lattice calculations. Our findings indicate that the previously estimated $1\%$ electromagnetic correction should be revised downward to $0.02\%$, a level of precision that aligns with current experimental uncertainties.

This paper introduces a novel deep learning architecture for image denoising that integrates residual connections with an identity branch. This dual-path design enables the network to learn both the residual and the original signal in parallel, offering superior adaptability to varying noise levels. Experimental results indicate that this approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art denoising techniques.

This paper investigates latent correlation-based multi-view learning (MCL) and self-guided MCL (SG-MCL) from the standpoint of identifiability. We establish that both SG-MCL and latent correlation-based MCL are identifiable under mild conditions. Furthermore, we introduce a new MCL variant, referred to as correlation-based self-guided MCL (CSG-MCL), which combines SG-MCL and latent correlation-based MCL. We demonstrate that CSG-MCL is identifiable under the same mild conditions applicable to its constituent methods. Additionally, we provide theoretical analysis of the convergence rates for both SG-MCL and CSG-MCL. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of our proposed CSG-MCL through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

We introduce a novel method for identifying galaxies with distinctive mid-infrared (MIR) colors, specifically targeting those with exceptionally high [24/8] values. By analyzing the [24/8] color distribution of the 2MASS-selected galaxy sample, we identified 1,000 candidates with [24/8] $\geq$ 3.0. These objects were cross-referenced with the WISE catalog to determine their [3.4/4.6] colors, revealing that 24% of the sample exhibits unusually red MIR colors (defined as [3.4/4.6] $\geq$ 0.5). These galaxies are predominantly found in the local universe (z < 0.05) and are characterized by high stellar mass, low star formation rates, and elevated dust temperatures. We propose that these galaxies represent a distinct population of dust-heated systems, likely driven by intense starbursts or active galactic nuclei (AGN). To further investigate this hypothesis, we examined the [3.4/4.6] color distribution of the 2MASS-selected sample, which showed a significant excess of red galaxies at [3.4/4.6] $\geq$ 0.5. We investigate how large language models (LLMs) can simulate human ethical judgment, specifically focusing on their ability to replicate the tendency to grant exceptions in moral reasoning. Using a dataset of 1,000 prompts and responses from the "Trolley Problem" (a classic moral dilemma), we analyzed both human and model responses to determine agreement on when exceptions apply. Our findings indicate that LLMs can accurately emulate human ethical judgment with 70% accuracy. Furthermore, we demonstrate that LLMs capture a critical human trait: the capacity to identify when standard rules should be overridden. Finally, we outline the specific types of exceptions that LLMs currently struggle to recognize.

We demonstrate that any valuation domain possessing a finite-dimensional ramification can be approached as a directed limit of unique factorization valuation domains that are complete intersection rings. Furthermore, this methodology extends to show that the class of complete valuation domains with residual fields of characteristic p constitutes an ind-category.

This study examines the two-dimensional Dirac equation in the presence of an electromagnetic field, specifically addressing the Coulomb potential. We derive a closed-form solution for the system's eigenfunctions and establish the critical limit for the fine-structure constant. Furthermore, we perform a quantitative analysis of the system's eigenvalues.

This study introduces a cooperative adaptive cruise control (CACC) framework designed to mitigate the impact of communication failures within a platoon. The proposed system employs a centralized Model Predictive Control (MPC) strategy, where the communication topology is structured as a directed graph representing inter-vehicle connections. The control objective is to maintain a fixed inter-vehicle distance while ensuring all vehicles track a desired reference speed. The MPC algorithm utilizes a linearized vehicle dynamics model and incorporates constraints for acceleration and velocity limits, alongside comfort requirements. The primary contribution of this work is the development of a control architecture that remains robust against communication link failures. The algorithm dynamically reconfigures the communication graph whenever a connection fails, thereby maintaining connectivity and enabling the entire platoon to achieve consensus in velocity and acceleration. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the proposed controller guarantees stability and convergence to the reference trajectory, provided the reconfigured communication graph remains connected. The efficacy of this approach is validated through simulation results.

In recent years, the social media landscape has been dominated by the rise of "fake news," which has had profound effects on society. This study introduces a novel approach to automatically detect trustworthy Twitter users, aiming to mitigate the spread of misinformation. We developed a new method that combines the strengths of both supervised and unsupervised learning to achieve this. Our experiments demonstrate that this hybrid approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art models. Furthermore, we conducted an in-depth analysis of the features that characterize credible news accounts.

This paper introduces $\pi$-ROAD, a learn-as-you-approach framework designed to optimize the performance of Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) applications. It specifically targets urgent data slices, which are critical for time-sensitive tasks such as collision avoidance and traffic signal coordination. The framework employs a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) agent to dynamically adjust the transmission rate of these slices, thereby enhancing overall network utility. To achieve this, $\pi$-ROAD utilizes a multi-agent architecture where each vehicle is equipped with a sensor array that captures environmental data and a processor that generates urgent slices. These slices are then transmitted to a central infrastructure node via a wireless channel. The node's primary function is to process these slices and disseminate relevant information to the vehicles. The study evaluates the framework's performance against a baseline approach that relies on a fixed transmission rate. Simulation results indicate that $\pi$-ROAD outperforms the baseline by increasing network utility by 10.5% and reducing the average delay experienced by urgent slices by 15.3%.

The rise of the fourth industrial revolution has spurred the development of advanced human-robot collaboration systems. However, current systems often fail to account for the human senses, which are crucial for safety and efficiency. This study introduces a haptic-based system designed to enhance human-robot collaboration by utilizing tactile feedback to improve safety. We developed a prototype system featuring a custom tactile display for the human forearm, which was tested in a simulated future factory environment. The results indicate that the system successfully conveys information through tactile feedback, thereby enhancing operational safety.

The swift advancement of autonomous vehicles (AVs) has sparked significant debate regarding their deployment in cities. This discussion is essential for addressing the complex socio-technical challenges inherent in urban environments. To navigate this complexity, we introduce a novel framework for analyzing AV deployment, which examines the interplay between socio-technical challenges and the AVs themselves. This approach enables a comprehensive analysis of the characteristics of both challenges and technology, facilitating the identification of appropriate strategies for AV integration within urban settings. We demonstrate the framework's utility by applying it to three key AV challenges: automated driving, automated parking, and ride-hailing.

This paper examines online caching within a framework where an online algorithm receives a probabilistic prediction regarding the likelihood of future requests. We introduce a novel algorithmic approach that leverages these predictions to achieve near-optimal online caching performance. Specifically, we demonstrate that the algorithm's competitive ratio is bounded by a function of the optimal offline solution's cost and the actual prediction error, thereby establishing a corresponding lower bound on prediction error to ensure a competitive ratio of at most $O(\log N)$. Furthermore, we prove that the algorithm's performance degrades gracefully as prediction accuracy diminishes.

Deep learning has become a dominant approach for medical image segmentation, yet current methods often struggle with real-time applications due to the computational demands of large-scale networks. To address this, we introduce the Trilateral Focus Network (TFN), a novel architecture designed for efficient, real-time segmentation. TFN integrates three key components: a novel multi-scale feature fusion module, a lightweight context aggregation module, and a novel feature refinement module. Experimental results on the ACDC and Kvasir datasets demonstrate that TFN achieves state-of-the-art performance in both accuracy and speed, surpassing existing methods. Furthermore, the network's robustness was validated on the MICCAI 2018 Pancreas Segmentation Challenge, where it secured a top-three ranking.

This study introduces the linearized off-shell framework for four-dimensional 4+7 supergravity, which serves as the non-linearizable limit of the 11D supergravity action when compactified on a 7-torus. By employing the 4+7 supergravity formalism, we establish the linearized action, field equations, and gauge symmetries in a manifestly covariant manner. Furthermore, we derive the linearized 4+7 supergravity field content and its corresponding gauge algebra by applying an off-shell extension of the 4+7 supergravity groupoid.

Data quality is a critical factor in machine learning, yet it is often overlooked in favor of model architecture and training strategies. This study introduces a novel approach to enhance data quality by leveraging the training dynamics of Gradient Boosting Decision Trees (GBDTs). We demonstrate that the training curves generated during the GBDT process can be utilized to identify and eliminate noisy data points. Furthermore, we introduce a new metric, the Noise Index, derived from these dynamics to assess data noise levels. This index facilitates the comparison of data quality across different datasets and tracks quality changes resulting from data augmentation. Ultimately, this work offers a fresh perspective on data quality assessment and augmentation, distinct from traditional methods that rely on model performance metrics.

We examine the unitary mapping between qubits within the context of the quantum Hall effect. This transformation is derived from the transformation of wave functions that leave the subspace of the quantum Hall effect invariant. We demonstrate that this qubit transformation is equivalent to the action of a specific operator on the vacuum state of the effect. Furthermore, this operator is linked to the creation of a localized hole in the qubit's wave function.

Pre-training has become a standard approach for developing large-scale language models, yet its effectiveness is hindered by the scarcity of high-quality data and the high costs associated with training. This work introduces a new pre-training strategy designed to enhance the efficiency of training large-scale language models. We propose a specialized architecture that utilizes a large-scale autoencoder to process noisy data, enabling the model to learn robust language structures. This method is trained on a massive corpus of 1.5 trillion tokens, resulting in a model that achieves state-of-the-art performance on various downstream tasks, including language modeling, machine translation, and text generation.

Quantum networks are essential for realizing the full potential of quantum information processing, yet their physical architecture is often obscured by the complexity of their design. This study introduces a method to infer quantum network topology using only local measurements, demonstrating that the network can be reconstructed from a single snapshot provided each node possesses sufficient quantum memory. This approach is validated through simulations on various quantum networks, including those with quantum repeaters, and is further supported by a mathematical proof establishing the method's scalability.

Information visualizations are designed to present data concisely and clearly, yet their effectiveness relies heavily on the user's ability to interpret them. This study examines how people understand these visualizations by analyzing crowdsourced natural language descriptions created by human participants. We gathered a dataset of 1,000 such descriptions for 100 distinct visualization visualizations from Turkers. Our analysis reveals that individuals typically focus on the most salient data points, prioritize visual elements like color and position, and often overlook the underlying data distribution. Furthermore, we observed that while descriptions of bar charts and line charts are more detailed, those of pie charts and scatter plots are less so. These findings offer valuable insights for designing visualizations that are both interpretable and comprehensible.

Counterfactual reasoning is essential for analyzing causal relationships, yet it is frequently hindered by the absence of data from the counterfactual world. This study addresses this limitation by introducing a framework that leverages distributional ambiguity to derive the most conservative inference. We propose a new ambiguity-adapted strategy for constructing counterfactuals, which utilizes the observed data distribution to define a set of plausible distributions. This set is then employed to calculate the necessary adjustments for generating counterfactual outcomes. We demonstrate that this ambiguity-informed approach yields a more robust basis for inference compared to traditional methods that rely on a single, specific strategy.

This study introduces a new benchmark for urban sound identification, featuring 10,000 audio clips from 8.5 hours of recordings across 10 distinct sound categories. We present results from several state-of-the-art deep learning models, including a new convolutional neural network architecture, and offer a detailed analysis of their performance. Additionally, we evaluate the impact of data augmentation techniques and provide a comprehensive comparison of various evaluation metrics.

We investigate supersymmetric AdS4 black holes within the framework of three-dimensional N=3 and N=4 gauged supergravities coupled to matter multiplets. Our analysis demonstrates that these black hole solutions are characterized by a specific set of half-BPS conditions. Furthermore, we derive an entropy formula applicable to half-BPS configurations in N=4 theories, which aligns with the N=4 entropy expression obtained in prior work.

Focal-plane sensors and processors (FPSs) are emerging as a promising alternative to conventional architectures for deep learning inference, offering superior energy efficiency and lower latency. These devices typically integrate an image sensor, an on-chip processor, and a specialized memory array. Although the processor and memory are designed to support convolutional neural networks (CNNs), the processor's instruction set is limited, and the memory architecture is not optimized for general-purpose tasks. Consequently, the processor can only execute specific operations, such as convolution, while the memory is restricted to storing convolutional weights. This paper introduces Cain, a compiler that automatically generates code for CNN inference on FPSs. Cain streamlines the development of CNNs by abstracting the underlying hardware details, allowing users to define network layers using high-level abstractions. The compiler then automatically optimizes the code for the FPS, including the generation of the necessary instruction sequence and the allocation of data within the memory array. Cain supports a broad spectrum of convolutional layers, including standard convolutions, depthwise convolutions, batch normalization, and ReLU activations. We evaluated Cain on the Convolutional Neural Network for Optical Character Recognition (CNN-OCR) and the MobileNet architecture using the ICDAR 2013 dataset. The results demonstrate that Cain achieves an accuracy of 99.2% for CNN-OCR and 94.1% for MobileNet, confirming the FPS's capability to effectively execute deep learning inference.

We examine how global symmetries break in Type IIB string theory compactifications on Calabi-Yau threefolds, specifically focusing on the resulting axion displacements driven by D3-brane instantons. Our analysis reveals that axion shifts can be described by a generalized theta-term, which is determined by a sum of products involving triple intersection numbers and generalized Chern-Simons numbers. This generalized theta-term is established as a topological invariant, remaining unchanged under continuous deformations of the underlying Calabi-Yau geometry. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this term can be eliminated via a field redefinition, thereby confirming that axion shifts remain unambiguous physical observables. Finally, we explore the implications of these findings for axion inflation models.

We introduce an algorithm designed to master simulated games by employing regret pruning to refine the policy. This pruning mechanism leverages reward signals from the simulator to eliminate suboptimal actions, thereby reducing the policy space. By applying this method to a suite of simulated games, we demonstrate that it can effectively learn high-performing policies. Furthermore, we illustrate that the technique is versatile and applicable to various pruning strategies.

This paper presents a new framework for Aristotle's modal syllogistic, designated as A-Syl, which interprets the system through a specific semantic model. We demonstrate the system's consistency and establish it as the appropriate semantic representation for both Boethius's and Armstrong's modal logic.

This study introduces a detection defect in quantum causal analysis, which can be exploited to generate false causal relationships. We demonstrate that this vulnerability is specific to the non-unitary nature of measurement operations. To address this, we propose a unitary-based measurement framework that effectively mitigates the identified attack.

This paper introduces a frame-level bit distribution algorithm designed to enhance the efficiency of High Efficiency Video Coding (HEVC) and H.265 video compression. The method employs a reinforcement learning (RL) framework utilizing a dual-critic structure, which integrates a temporal critic to optimize for long-term objectives and a frame-level critic to address immediate goals. By leveraging these two critics, the algorithm balances long-term and short-term rewards, thereby improving the overall compression efficiency of HEVC streams.

Cutting plane methods are widely used in optimization to enhance the efficiency of solving large-scale problems. However, the effectiveness of these approaches relies heavily on the quality of generated cuts, which is determined by the selection strategy. While existing techniques often select cuts by evaluating immediate benefits—such as the reduction in the objective function—they fail to account for the long-term impact on the overall optimization process. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that learns cutting plane strategies by imitating experts who make decisions based on future outcomes. Specifically, we utilize a neural network to model the policy of an expert agent trained via reinforcement learning, which itself uses Monte Carlo Tree Search to anticipate the long-term consequences of specific cuts. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in terms of both the quality of cuts and the overall optimization performance.

We report on the superconducting properties of the doped Weyl semimetal Mo$_{0.9}$Ir$_{0.1}$Te$_{2}$, which exhibits a critical temperature of $T_c = 2.5$ K. The material's electronic structure is characterized by a robust Fermi surface composed of electron pockets at the $\Gamma$ point and hole pockets at the $Z$ point, alongside a substantial Hall coefficient that indicates a high carrier density. Notably, the Hall coefficient's sign inversion at low temperatures, alongside the observed superconductivity, suggests that breaking inversion symmetry via doping induces Weyl nodes. Furthermore, the superconducting gap is highly anisotropic, with a maximum value of $2\Delta_0/k_B T_c \approx 4.5$ and a minimum of $2\Delta_{\min}/k_B T_c \approx 0.5$.

This paper introduces a deep learning approach utilizing Natural Language Processing (NLP) to automatically categorize bug reports. The study proposes a method for classifying bug descriptions by integrating word embeddings with Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. The system's efficacy was validated using a dataset of 1,000 bug descriptions from the Eclipse Java project, where it achieved an F1-score of 0.84.

We investigate the anisotropic graphene model, which features a square lattice with two atoms per unit cell and incorporates nearest-neighbor hopping along the sides of the square as well as a weaker hopping across the diagonals. The system's phase diagram is determined by the two hopping parameters alongside the applied electric field. The resulting band structure is characterized by two Dirac cones positioned at the corners of the Brillou zone, separated by a tunable gap. The study examines the system's ground state across the complete parameter range, identifying three distinct phases: a fully gapped insulator, a fully metallic conductor, and a semimetallic state. The semimetallic phase is defined by the presence of isolated Dirac points within the band gap.

Recent advancements in Remotely-Supervised Named Entity Recognition (RSNER) have primarily focused on enhancing the precision of relation type predictions. However, RSNER systems typically rely on a single teacher-student architecture, which often fails to fully leverage the complementary strengths of multiple distinct models. To address this, we introduce a new adaptive teacher learning framework that integrates an ensemble of specialized students, each trained on different subsets of the data. This approach leverages the unique advantages of each model to boost prediction accuracy. Furthermore, we develop a fine-grained student ensemble strategy that aggregates predictions from these individual models to further refine performance. Extensive experiments on established benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques, achieving improvements of up to 2.4% in F1-score.

The rise of social media has significantly boosted the tourism sector, as travelers increasingly utilize platforms like Twitter to share their experiences. This study introduces a comprehensive framework designed to extract and analyze these travel-related posts. We developed a specific set of tourism experience tags and tested the method's efficacy through a case study focused on the city of Venice. Our findings demonstrate that the approach successfully extracts tourism narratives from Twitter, offering valuable insights for both the tourism industry and social media researchers.

We analyze the characteristics of this specific type of circular orbit and compare them with standard centered counterparts. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the infall of matter along these off-center paths generates a distinct type of gravitational wave, offering a potential avenue for future observational detection.

This study introduces a backward simulation technique for estimating the trajectories of multiple objects. Unlike conventional forward simulations that assume specific object behaviors, our approach leverages the fact that physical laws operate bidirectionally to infer past movements. By utilizing a camera to measure object positions, we apply this method to predict how objects will move upon impact with a target. To validate the approach, we conducted an experiment involving a steel ball striking a steel plate, comparing the results against data from a high-speed camera.

This paper introduces a new method for evaluating the stability of multi-infeed grids connected via Voltage Source Converters (VSCs). The approach relies on the eigenvalues derived from a system admittance matrix, which incorporates the dynamic characteristics of the VSC control systems. The method's validity is confirmed through a case study involving a four-infeed system, with results compared against the multi-infeed equivalent circuit.

This study examines the characteristics of online signature templates, specifically focusing on the uniqueness, complexity, and repeatability of loops. We introduce a method to quantify the complexity of these signatures, which is defined as the weighted average of the lengths of the individual segments that make up the signature. Our findings indicate that signatures created by the same individual are highly distinctive, whereas those from different individuals are significantly different. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the complexity of signatures varies among people and can serve as a metric to differentiate between signers.

This paper presents two geometric frameworks for interpreting Hardy sums. The first framework models these sums as weighted counts of lattice points situated within a simplex, while the second interprets them as weighted averages of points in a hypercube.

We introduce a novel architecture for reinforcement learning (RL) agents that integrates the stability and adaptability of deep learning with the robustness of symbolic RL. This system utilizes a differentiable, context-sensitive symbolic layer to generate a high-level, interpretable reasoning model, which then guides a low-level symbolic RL agent. This hierarchical structure enables the agents to master intricate tasks, such as playing Tic-Tac-Toe, by leveraging a persistent memory of contextual variables to capture long-term dependencies. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our approach naturally supports multi-agent interactions, such as Tic-Tac-Toe, by treating the opponent as a dynamic element of the context.

This study introduces a novel, end-to-end deep learning framework designed to estimate the 3D poses of human joints from video sequences. The architecture employs dilated convolutional layers to extract features from individual frames, followed by a recurrent neural network (RNN) that integrates information across time. To further enhance pose estimation accuracy, attention mechanisms are incorporated into the RNN. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, achieving a substantial improvement in pose estimation accuracy.

The CZTI instrument aboard the AstroSat mission, equipped with a collimator, functions as an X-ray collimated detector capable of monitoring occultations by celestial bodies to generate occultation curves. These curves allow for the determination of the angular resolution and energy response of the collimator. By leveraging these occultation curves, we can detect X-ray sources that are undetectable through direct observation, thereby enabling the construction of an all-sky X-ray survey. Furthermore, this approach facilitates the identification of X-ray sources that are obscured from the collimator's direct line of sight.

Blockchain technology has gained significant traction in recent years, particularly for its ability to facilitate secure, decentralized, and distributed data storage. However, the field of blockchain research currently lacks a unified framework for analyzing and comparing the efficiency of various protocols. This paper introduces such a framework, designed to evaluate the efficiency of blockchain systems by examining their underlying distributed ledger technologies (DLTs). We demonstrate that, under specific conditions, the efficiency of a DLT can be represented as a weighted sum of the computational costs associated with its constituent algorithms. Furthermore, we apply this framework to assess the efficiency of several prominent DLTs, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Ripple. Our findings indicate that the proposed method is both practical and effective for measuring the efficiency of existing and emerging DLTs.

We investigate the mass spectra of doubly heavy tetraquarks ($QQ\bar{q}\bar{q}$) within a framework that incorporates a significant chromomagnetic interaction. Our analysis reveals that this interaction substantially influences the mass spectra, particularly for states with spin $S=0$ and $1$. Consequently, the predicted masses for these doubly heavy tetraquarks are notably higher than those derived from previous studies that neglected such an interaction.

We investigate the possibility that the electroweak vacuum instability sets a natural limit on the energy scale of the Standard Model (SM) by preventing the Higgs field from entering the true vacuum up to Planck-scale distances. This mechanism imposes a lower bound on the Higgs mass, expressed as $m_{\rm H} \geq 130$ GeV, where the analysis incorporates uncertainties in Planck-scale physics. Consequently, the SM remains viable only if the Higgs mass is below this threshold, a condition that aligns with recent experimental findings.

This paper examines the relationship between a $q$-logarithmic Sobolev inequality and a $p$-Talagrand inequality within the framework of weighted Carnot structures. We establish that a $q$-logarithmic Sobolev inequality holds if and only if a specific condition involving a distance function is met, a criterion that is equivalent to the associated $p$-Talagrand inequality.

This study investigates the application of information geometry within Bayesian inference, specifically focusing on deriving posterior distributions from prior distributions and likelihood functions using Bregman divergences. By employing an appropriate Bregman divergence, this framework allows for the representation of Bayesian inference as a minimization problem. The work further examines the characteristics of these optimal posterior distributions and establishes a connection between this minimal Bregman divergence approach and standard Bayesian inference.

This study introduces a novel approach to reconstructing 3D geometry and rendering novel views for dynamic scenes from sparse, in-the-wild monocular footage. By leveraging a combination of 2D and 3D cues, our method utilizes a neural radiance field (NeRF) to synthesize novel perspectives of the environment. To achieve this, we employ a two-stage pipeline: first, we estimate 3D camera poses and a time-varying depth map for every frame using a Siamese network trained on the NeRF-Studio dataset. Next, we integrate these depth maps with image features to train a differentiable volumetric rendering network, which generates a unified NeRF representation of the scene. Experimental results demonstrate that our technique successfully produces high-fidelity view synthesis and accurate 3D geometry for dynamic environments, even when trained on extremely sparse data.

This study examines a spectral statistic in quantum graphs, previously linked to zeta functions of zolotaryuk, by demonstrating that it can be expressed through the zeta function associated with a specific periodic orbit set. This representation allows the statistic to be written as a sum involving periodic orbit periods and their respective indices. Furthermore, we prove that this index-based periodic orbit sum converges for all connected quantum graphs, provided their total length remains finite.

This study introduces a novel technique for determining the intervals of periodic variable stars. The method involves constructing a light curve from observations and then generating a series of synthetic light curves by shifting the original data. The original star's interval is identified as the shift amount that maximizes the correlation coefficient between the real and synthetic curves. This approach was tested on the Kepler dataset, specifically on 1,000 stars with known intervals, and successfully recovered the true intervals in 99.9% of cases.

Negative imaginary (NI) systems are a class of systems that exhibit stable equilibrium when connected in a feedback loop with a suitable NI controller. This paper introduces the concept of a "near-ordered" negative imaginary (NNI) system, defined as a system whose state-space matrix can be partitioned into an NNI submatrix and a remainder. The authors demonstrate that the stability properties of an NNI system extend to feedback interconnections involving NNIs, provided the controller is designed based on the NNI submatrix. Furthermore, the paper presents a new algorithm for determining the closest NNI system to a given one. This method is applied to the design of near-optimal controllers for feedback control of NNIs.

This paper introduces a continual learning approach designed for automatic speech recognition (ASR) that eliminates the need for transcription templates. The method involves training a model on a specific language and then progressively adding new languages, with the objective of minimizing the resulting word error rate (WER) without retraining from scratch. The study evaluates the efficacy of continual learning strategies, including EWC, a combination of EWC and a replay buffer, and a combination of EWC and data augmentation. The findings indicate that the best performance is achieved by the method utilizing both replay and data augmentation, which reduces WER by 10% relative to a standard baseline trained solely on the initial language.

Code-switching, the practice of alternating between two or more languages within a single conversation, is a prevalent linguistic phenomenon. This study addresses the challenge of sentiment analysis for code-switching text, a task that is particularly difficult because it involves mixed languages. We introduce a straightforward deep learning model designed to classify sentiment in such contexts. The system was evaluated on the "Spanglish" subset of the 2020 IAC-SEMESTER 9 dataset, which contains Spanglish conversations. The model achieved an F1 score of 0.70, a result that aligns with the performance of other state-of-the-art methods.

This study explores a low-scale seesaw framework where the standard Type-I mechanism is extended with an additional scalar singlet, $S$, which drives mass splitting in the neutrino mass matrix via radiative corrections. This splitting is generated through a three-loop diagram, necessitating the inclusion of a top quark within the loop. We demonstrate that the model's parameters can be constrained using existing experimental data, specifically the measured Higgs boson mass and its total decay width, alongside the model's capacity to account for neutrinoless double beta decay. Furthermore, we analyze the model's viability in generating neutrino masses and leptogenesis, while also investigating its potential to explain dark matter.

We introduce a neural network designed to predict user responses, utilizing an item embedding vector as input. This model is trained on click-through rate (CTR) data derived from historical user interactions. The core innovation lies in constructing the item vector representation through a combination of two neural networks: one processes the user's search query, while the other analyzes the item's metadata. This dual-network approach is particularly effective for scenarios involving sparse data, where the item response rate is low. By leveraging metadata, the system can generate embeddings for items lacking direct interaction history, thereby enhancing the model's ability to predict responses.

This study introduces a robust active and passive beamforming design for IRS-supported cell-free networks (CFNs) that accounts for both hardware imperfections and channel estimation errors. The objective is to maximize the minimum user rate under these conditions. To address this, we first formulate an equivalent non-convex fractional programming problem, which is then transformed into a tractable form using the weighted minimum mean-square error (WMMSE) framework. Subsequently, we apply the successive convex approximation (SCA) method to iteratively optimize active beamforming vectors, passive beamforming vectors, and weighted factors. Furthermore, we propose a distributed IRS phase shift optimization algorithm that requires no user-specific data. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the proposed robust joint design significantly outperforms existing benchmarks in terms of fairness and robustness.

Branch prediction is a critical component of modern processors, and dynamic branch prediction specifically aims to enhance performance by forecasting the direction of control flow based on recent program execution. This survey examines recent deep learning approaches to dynamic branch prediction, detailing the data collection and processing techniques used to generate training sets, as well as the specific deep learning architectures employed for branch prediction.

This paper introduces a deep convolutional neural network (DCNN) designed to facilitate active camera control through imitation. The system utilizes a network of convolutional layers to process visual inputs and generate corresponding control commands. To enhance the model's robustness, we incorporate a data augmentation strategy. Furthermore, we propose a novel loss function that integrates both image-level and control-level information to improve the DCNN's performance. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods.

This paper investigates the partition function of a simple one-dimensional spin system featuring nearest-neighbor interactions, specifically focusing on the Solid-On-Solid model. We derive an explicit formula for the partition function using a method based on a second-order, non-linear difference equation. Furthermore, we analyze the high-temperature and low-energy regimes of the model, as well as its behavior when the boundary conditions are altered.

This study introduces a novel scheme for resonance-based power transfer utilizing entangled photons, where the donor and acceptor possess identical energy levels despite existing in arbitrary media. The research demonstrates that the entanglement between photon pairs allows these donator and acceptor to function as if they reside in the same medium, thereby enabling efficient power transfer regardless of the surrounding dielectric environment.

This study investigates the strong interactions between charmed and bottom mesons and light vector mesons within the framework of QCD sum rules. By employing the robust coupling constants derived from these rules, we analyze the semileptonic decays of $D$ and $B$ mesons. Our findings indicate that the axial vector form factors at zero momentum transfer, $A_1(0)$, are approximately 0.99 for $D$ decays and 0.97 for $B$ decays. These values align well with the predictions of the Standard Model's Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (CKM) mechanism.
This document provides a brief overview of the neutrino experiments set to commence operation in the near future.

This study examines the properties of linear regression coefficients when used to estimate causal effects in scenarios involving multiple confounders. We demonstrate that these coefficients are consistent estimators of the true causal effects, provided the model is correctly specified. However, if the linear model is misspecified, the resulting estimates converge to a specific weighted average of the actual causal effects. These weights are determined by the covariance between the true and estimated confounders and their regression residuals. Furthermore, we establish sufficient conditions ensuring these weights are non-negative. Finally, we apply these theoretical findings to linear regression estimators that incorporate propensity scores.

This paper introduces a novel, WAMS-driven, model-free wide-area damping control strategy for grid-connected voltage source converters (GVCs). The proposed approach leverages Phasor Measurement Units (PMUs) to capture real-time dynamic responses of VSCs, subsequently utilizing a data-driven algorithm to derive control parameters that optimize damping performance. The control scheme is validated through a case study involving a 1000 MW VSC-HVDC link connecting the Western and Eastern US power grids. The results demonstrate that the proposed control effectively mitigates low-frequency oscillations, thereby enhancing the overall stability of the interconnected system.

We investigate the steady-state behavior of two atoms coupled to a single-mode waveguide, where both are excited by a laser. By deriving the steady-state photon statistics, we demonstrate that the system can be steered between superradiant and subradiant regimes by adjusting the laser detuning and the atom's separation. Furthermore, we show that the system's steady-state photon statistics can be tuned from thermal to non-thermal distributions by modifying the atom-atom distance and the ratio of the laser Rabi frequency to the single-atom Rabi frequency.

This study examines the asymptotic stability of a kink within the sine-Gordon equation, subject to a weak, periodic transverse perturbation that varies with small amplitude and frequency. The kink is known to exhibit internal modes, which are characterized by a decay rate proportional to the perturbation frequency. The analysis demonstrates that when the frequency of the external force coincides with one of these internal mode frequencies, the kink fails to remain stable. The resulting displacement grows linearly with time, scaled by the magnitude of the perturbation amplitude. The paper further establishes that this instability is absent if the frequency of the driving force is rationally independent of the kink's internal modes.

The J-PARC facility in Japan is set to commence operations in 2021, with a primary aim of investigating the fundamental nature of hadrons. This initiative includes a dedicated hadron physics program utilizing a 30 GeV proton beam to generate high-energy meson and nuclear targets, thereby enabling the exploration of the nuclear reaction environment at the GeV scale. This overview outlines the J-PARC hadron physics program and examines its potential to advance our understanding of the color transparency phenomenon.

Consistency regularization has recently emerged as a promising technique for unsupervised pre-training, leveraging the principle that minor input perturbations should yield identical outputs. This paper introduces a novel regularization method designed to enhance the robustness of pre-training models. Our approach utilizes an adversarially perturbed input to enforce consistency, specifically targeting the most informative dimensions of the discrete feature space. By incorporating a virtual adversarial discrete disturbance, we ensure that the model maintains consistent predictions despite perturbations applied to the most discriminative parts of the feature representation. Extensive experiments on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets demonstrate that this method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches.

Detecting polyps in endoscopic videos is a critical task for diagnosing colorectal cancer. However, the presence of significant camera movements and lighting fluctuations in endoscopic footage, combined with the small size and low contrast of polyps, makes video-based detection particularly difficult. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel spatio-temporal feature transformation (STFT) module designed to enhance the extraction of spatial and temporal features. This module employs a multi-frame cooperative strategy to aggregate information from multiple frames, thereby improving the quality of the extracted features. Furthermore, we utilize a dedicated temporal attention mechanism to capture long-term dependencies across frames. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on the Kvasir and CVC-ClinicDB datasets. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/zhengyu1996/STFNet.

Stream sampling is a critical technique for monitoring water quality, yet it faces significant challenges due to the high velocity of flow and the necessity for rapid decisions. These constraints often prevent the use of traditional sampling methods, which typically rely on fixed equal likelihood thresholds. To address this, we introduce a new sequential unequal likelihood (SUL) algorithm designed to enhance sampling efficiency. This approach allows for the dynamic adjustment of the sampling window based on real-time data, enabling the system to sample more frequently when water quality deteriorates and less often when conditions remain stable. We developed a theoretical framework to analyze the SUL algorithm's performance and validated its effectiveness through both simulations and real-world data.

The $rp$-process, which occurs in the most proton-rich nuclei, is a critical component of stellar nucleosynthesis. A pivotal aspect of this process is the hindrance point bypass, which marks the transition from $\beta$-delayed neutron emission to $\beta$-delayed proton emission. This study presents the first experimental determination of the $T_z$ = 1/2 hindrance point for $^{57}$Zn, achieved by measuring its proton emission branching ratio using the GANIL-INDRA setup. The findings indicate that the $T_z$ = 1/2 hindrance point for $^{57}$Zn lies at approximately 1.5 MeV above the proton separation energy, aligning with recent theoretical predictions. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that the $T_z$ = 1/2 nuclei in the $Z$ = 28–30 region exhibit proton emission branching ratios comparable to those of $T_z$ = 3/2 nuclei in the $Z$ = 26–28 region.

We demonstrate that within a generic elliptic fibration of Poincaré modular surface, the set of points with complex multiplication (CM) lying on an elliptic curve of low degree is finite. This finding extends Manin's classical theorem regarding rational curves on Shimura varieties to the realm of degree one curves. The proof relies on the principle of effective intersection for these specific elliptic curves, a technique derived from the work of Avanzi, Lelli-Chiesa, and Zureick-Brown.

This study reports on the analysis of Very High Energy (VHE) gamma-ray data collected by the VERITAS telescope array, which has been observing a subset of northern-sky pulsars since 2007. The investigation employed a novel search technique designed to identify gamma-ray emission originating from the immediate surroundings of pulsars. The analysis focused on a sample of 17 pulsars, including 11 with known gamma-ray emission and 6 candidates lacking such prior evidence. The results indicate no significant detection of VHE gamma-ray emission around any of the target pulsars. Consequently, the study establishes upper limits on the fluxes for these sources, which are then compared against theoretical predictions.

This study examines the asymptotic behavior of reaction-diffusion models incorporating nonlocal boundary conditions within domains of irregular geometry. We establish findings regarding the existence of boundary-aware, nonlocal attractors, specifically addressing scenarios where the domain exhibits fractal characteristics and the boundary possesses a fractional dimension.

We introduce a machine learning (ML) algorithm designed to identify extragalactic Ultra-Compact Dwarfs (UCDs) and Globular Groups (GGs) within the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) database. This method utilizes a novel set of features derived from the photometric and morphological properties of galaxies, including the Galaxy Morphology Classification (GAMOG) system. GAMOG, a convolutional neural network (CNN) trained on the Galaxy Zoo 8 dataset, assigns morphological labels to galaxies. Our feature selection process incorporates GAMOG's confidence scores and the probability distributions of its output classes. Additionally, we integrate color, luminosity, and morphological metrics from the Galaxy Zoo 8, 9, and 10 datasets. Our model achieves a 90% detection rate for extragalactic UCDs and GGs, with a 90% purity rate. We also demonstrate that integrating GAMOG significantly enhances the model's performance. Finally, we outline the interpretability of our ML approach using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to identify the most critical features for classification.

This paper examines the role of simulation in developing suggestion systems, highlighting how such models can effectively evaluate diverse candidate ranking strategies. By analyzing real-world scenarios from our industry experience, we demonstrate the application of these simulations to optimize various hyperparameters, ranging from the count of suggested items to the volume of information retrieved from databases.

This paper introduces a robust, nonparametric large-sample test for the mean applicable to truncated samples derived from extremely heavy-tailed distributions. The test's power function, along with its asymptotic behavior under local alternatives, is analyzed using the method of stable processes. Notably, the proposed approach demonstrates superior performance compared to standard methods that rely on empirical exceedances over thresholds. The efficacy of these findings is validated through both simulation studies and an empirical analysis of data from the 2011 East Japan Earthquake.

Motor imagery-based Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) systems are increasingly utilized for communication and control, yet their effectiveness is often hindered by the low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of electroencephalography (EEG) signals. This study introduces a new convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture designed to enhance motor imagery classification by leveraging Sinc-based filters. The proposed Sinc-CNN outperforms standard CNNs and established BCI methods in classifying EEG data from a dataset of 10 subjects performing left and right motor imagery tasks. The model's efficacy stems from the Sinc function's ability to effectively capture the spectral characteristics of EEG signals. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that the Sinc function's parameters can be optimized to further boost classification performance.

We introduce a specific correspondence linking the isometric group of $AdS_2$ to the noncommutative $AdS_2$ (NAD$S_2$) model. This mapping connects the NAD$S_2$ coordinates to the group elements of $ISO(2,2)$, thereby allowing the model's dynamics to be expressed in terms of group variables. We demonstrate that this approach yields a consistent formulation of the NAD$S_2$ system and establish a direct link between the model's Hamiltonian and the Casimir operator of $ISO(2,2)$.

Kidney transplant recipients face a significantly lower risk of death compared to those on the waiting list, yet many remain on the registry for extended periods due to a shortage of available organs. While recent policy changes in the US allow non-matched donors to be added to the pool of compatible organs, these donations are not always accepted by all transplant centers. This paper introduces a mathematical model designed to determine the optimal strategy for accepting or declining unmatched donor kidneys. The model accounts for the fact that a transplanted organ does not guarantee a cure, as recipients may still die from other causes, and that a transplanted patient can revert to the pool of those on the waiting list if the organ fails. Furthermore, the model incorporates the possibility that a patient currently on the waiting list can receive a donated organ later. The study demonstrates that the optimal acceptance policy is characterized by a threshold approach based on the number of organs already held by the recipient system.

This study introduces a hybrid approach that merges the HMM and LSTM architectures to enhance the performance of sequential data analysis. The proposed model leverages the LSTM's capability to generate precise probability distributions for hidden states, which are subsequently utilized to drive the HMM framework. Evaluated on the IMDB movie review sentiment dataset, the hybrid model achieved an accuracy of 88.89%, surpassing the standalone HMM (70.00%) and LSTM (60.00%) models.

This study examines generalized Volterra integral operators acting on weighted Bergman spaces, alongside their associated induced Toeplitz operators. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for both operators to exhibit boundedness, compactness, and the behavior of being in finite or zero classes. Additionally, the text explores the spectrum and essential spectrum of these induced Toeplitz operators.

We present a strategy for efficiently compressing multilingual models across multiple tasks, specifically utilizing BERT and RoBERTa. By applying the knowledge distillation method described by Sanh et al. (2019), we compress a full RoBERTa model into a smaller variant containing 110 million parameters. This distilled model retains 90% of the original performance on the MMLU benchmark while achieving a 5x reduction in model size.

The widespread adoption of smartphones and the Internet of Things (IoT) has led to a surge in data generation, creating a critical need for efficient and scalable data access methods. This paper offers a personal perspective on recent advancements in data access, specifically examining mobile computing, mobile cloud computing, and fog computing. It further explores the integration of these frameworks with emerging technologies such as Blockchain, the Internet of Everything (IoE), and the Internet of Vehicles (IoV). Additionally, the study addresses key challenges including security, privacy, and the Internet of Everything (IoE), while also surveying current research trends and highlighting open research questions.

This paper introduces a decomposition of the Richelot isogeny specifically for Jacobians of hyperelliptic curves defined over finite fields. This decomposition facilitates the construction of specific isogeny classes and enables the computation of Richelot isogenies within genera exceeding two. Furthermore, we provide an explicit construction of the Richelot isogeny class and a generalized form of the Howe curve applicable to these decomposed hyperelliptic Jacobians.

We report the discovery of three magnetic hot subdwarf stars, designated SDSS J1228+1020, SDSS J1228+1020, and SDSS J1228+1020, which exhibit significant rotational splitting in their pulsation frequencies. These stars display a characteristic period spacing of approximately 10 minutes, consistent with that of non-magnetic hot subdwarfs. However, their rotational splitting values are notably higher than expected for non-magnetic counterparts, suggesting that the observed splitting is driven by strong internal rotation. We propose that the magnetic fields in these objects were generated via a merger event, a scenario that also accounts for their rapid rotation. This finding supports the hypothesis that the formation of hot subdwarf B stars (sdB) through mergers is a common evolutionary pathway.

This paper presents WikiHist.html, an HTML-based collection of every revision history page from the English Wikipedia. These pages are designed to facilitate efficient data extraction and analysis of edit histories. The work includes a detailed examination of the dataset's characteristics and provides a comparison with a similar study by M. H. Kim et al. regarding its findings.

Twisted bilayers of magnetic materials offer a versatile framework for investigating emergent phenomena, including topological textures and novel phases driven by twisting. This study examines the interplay between topological textures and twisted bilayers in a two-dimensional Ising ferromagnet. We demonstrate that, at specific twist angles, the system spontaneously forms a polar meron-antimeron lattice characterized by a distinctive, long-range dipolar order. This configuration represents a new type of topological texture that can be identified through its unique magnetic signature. Furthermore, we show that these polar lattice structures can be readily tuned by adjusting the system's temperature or twist angle.

This paper introduces a new framework for theoretical physics, specifically tailored for scenarios where a 3D physical space is embedded within a higher-dimensional manifold. The discussion begins by examining the historical context of this formalism, followed by an analysis of the implications for physical laws and the nature of physical entities. The work concludes by addressing the cosmological constant problem and offering a novel perspective on dark matter.

We present a novel method for controlling colloidal movement within nematic liquid crystals by utilizing surface topography. Our findings indicate that wall undulations can generate distinct flow patterns, specifically inducing the formation of nematic textures characterized by alternating bands of $+1/2$ and $-1/2$ topological defects. These defects serve as pathways for the alignment of colloidal particles, thereby dictating their trajectories. Furthermore, we demonstrate that by adjusting the wavelength of the surface roughness, one can modulate the spacing between these trajectory lanes.

This study examines how asteroid shape affects the outcome of close planetary flybys. We demonstrate that the asteroid's elongation is a critical factor in determining whether a disruption occurs, with elongated bodies being more prone to disruption than spherical ones. Our analysis indicates that the degree of shape elongation is a key variable in predicting the disruption threshold, suggesting that disruption can happen at higher velocities for elongated asteroids compared to spherical ones. These findings are supported by a new analytical model that incorporates asteroid shape, which aligns well with our N-body simulations.

We introduce a quantum algorithm designed to efficiently sample rare conformational transitions within molecular systems. This approach utilizes a variational quantum eigensolver to determine the system's energy spectrum and a quantum phase estimation technique to calculate the transition rates of infrequent events. We demonstrate that the algorithm's quantum resource requirements scale linearly with the number of transition states and polynomials in the number of electronic orbitals, offering a significant improvement over the cubic scaling found in classical methods. Furthermore, we identify that the algorithm is resilient to both mid-circuit measurement errors and specific non-Markovian noise, provided the energy spectrum remains sufficiently resolved.

We introduce MAPPIES, a novel Monte Carlo tool designed to simulate the radiative processes of inverse Compton scattering within the framework of the LHAASO experiment. This software is specifically tailored for modeling the scattering of high-energy photons by relativistic electrons in the magnetospheres of pulsars and black holes. The code's primary objective is to facilitate the interpretation of LHAASO's observations of TeV gamma-ray emission from these sources. We present the first simulations of inverse Compton scattering in the magnetospheres of neutron stars, specifically focusing on the Crab pulsar. These simulations demonstrate that the resulting TeV gamma-ray emission is highly sensitive to the polarization state of the primary electron beam. Furthermore, we examine the impact of varying the scattering angle on the spectral characteristics of the emitted radiation.

The Arctic Ocean's sea ice thickness distribution (SITD) is a critical indicator of the region's cryosphere state, yet its seasonal evolution remains poorly understood. This study utilizes the Community Earth System Model (CESM) to investigate the annual cycle of SITD, specifically examining the impacts of sea ice dynamics and thermodynamics. Our analysis reveals that the model accurately simulates the seasonal development of the SITD, with the ice thickness exceeding 1 m in the northern Arctic during winter and remaining ice-free in the south. Furthermore, the study finds that the thermodynamic processes governing the SITD are more significant than dynamic factors, particularly during winter.

We present a novel technique for computing the Weierstrass semigroup at a solitary point on maximal curves, which serves as an extension of the method developed by Kato and the second author. This approach is utilized to determine the Weierstrass semigroups at multiple points on specific maximal curves that encompass non-Weierstrass points; notably, these curves cannot be subcovered by the Hermitian curve.

This survey provides a comprehensive overview of recent advancements in singing voice synthesis (SVS), a field that has seen rapid evolution driven by deep learning. While earlier SVS methods relied on hand-crafted features, current approaches predominantly utilize deep learning architectures. This article examines the latest deep learning-based SVS systems, covering their underlying architectures, training methodologies, and evaluation metrics. Additionally, we address key research challenges and potential future directions for SVS.

We introduce NIPS4Bplus, a richly annotated dataset comprising 1,000 bird species, which expands upon the original NIPS4B collection by incorporating 200 additional species. This dataset features 100 hours of recordings captured across 100 distinct locations in the United Kingdom. The audio files are meticulously annotated with labels for species identity, specific calls, and temporal boundaries. We have also generated a subset of this data to support the development of a bird sound segmentation model.

Event cameras are emerging as a promising technology for robotics and computer vision, offering a unique alternative to conventional frame-based imaging. These sensors detect changes in pixel luminance rather than capturing full images, resulting in data streams that are sparse, asynchronous, and event-driven. However, manufacturing tolerances and environmental factors can cause significant variations in sensitivity and response latency across individual pixels, which hinders the extraction of meaningful information. This paper introduces a novel method to calibrate event cameras by estimating and correcting these sensitivity and latency discrepancies. Our approach utilizes a rotating checkerboard to generate data, from which we derive a robust cost function to optimize the estimation of pixel-level sensitivity and time-to-luminance parameters. Experiments demonstrate that this technique effectively normalizes event camera output, thereby enhancing the quality of downstream tasks.

Graphs serve as a versatile data structure capable of modeling diverse real-world entities and their interconnections, making graph analysis a foundational pillar of data science. This field has garnered significant attention from both academia and industry, driving the development of numerous algorithms and applications. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of graph analysis, encompassing its background, core concepts, and a wide array of use cases. We begin by defining graph analysis and delineating its fundamental concepts, followed by an examination of the primary data structures and models employed for representing graphs. Furthermore, we introduce a taxonomy of graph analysis, detailing the corresponding algorithms, applications, and underlying data models. The article concludes by identifying current limitations and outlining promising future research directions.

We introduce a novel exceptional compilation for the $\Sigma _{ 2 }$ region of the universal gate set comprising single-qubit gates and the T gate. This compilation consists of a sequence of 10 two-qubit CNOT gates paired with one-qubit gates drawn from an $E(2)$ subgroup of $SU(2)$, parameterized by five real numbers. This result is significant because it is the first known compilation for $\Sigma _{ 2 }$ utilizing an $E(2)$ subgroup, a method that is particularly valuable for quantum devices employing photonic qubits.

This paper introduces a novel method for 3D instrument tracking during retinal surgery, utilizing a spotlight to project a light stripe onto the instrument. A camera captures this stripe, which is subsequently reconstructed into 3D space via a calibrated system comprising the camera and the spotlight. The process involves generating a camera model from the spotlight, calculating the 3D stripe, and determining the instrument's position by finding the intersection of this 3D line with a sphere representing all feasible positions. The system's accuracy was validated through experiments, yielding a tracking error of 1.1 mm.

This paper presents two distinct formulas for computing $F$-polynomials, which are integral to the transformation of Kac-Moody skein algebras into their quantum cluster analogues. The first formula relies on a presentation of a specific monoid derived from the Coxeter group, while the second utilizes a presentation based on a related monoid of a Coxeter group.

This paper examines the current state of passwordless authentication, specifically focusing on the FIDO2 standard. It outlines the technical principles behind FIDO2, analyzes its pros and cons, and highlights the challenges involved in deploying the technology. The discussion also covers the necessary conditions for adoption, including user education, and concludes with a summary of FIDO2's future trajectory.

We examine a Wigner-Weyl calculus adapted for the phase space of relativistic Dirac particles on a lattice. This formulation relies on the finite-dimensional Dirac operator, $D$, which serves as the square root of the discrete Laplacian, $D^2$. We establish a Weyl-Weyl calculus within the framework of the Fock space generated by $L^2(\mathbb{Z}^d)$, where $d$ denotes the spatial dimension. The approach utilizes the spectral projections of $D$ to define Weyl symbols and operators, thereby extending the standard finite lattice Dirac operator formalism. We demonstrate that the calculus's fundamental properties hold, including the characterization of the fundamental Weyl-Weyl transform as an integral operator featuring a kernel expressed via the Green function of $D$. Furthermore, we prove that the trace of any operator within this calculus can be computed using the integral of its associated Weyl symbol.

YouTube serves as a primary source of entertainment and information for users worldwide. However, the platform's algorithmic curation can inadvertently lead to problematic viewing habits, such as excessive binge-watching. This study examines how users perceive their agency regarding their YouTube experience, specifically analyzing the impact of personalized recommendations versus on-demand search functionality. Findings indicate that while users generally feel in control of their usage, this perception is significantly stronger when utilizing the search feature compared to relying solely on recommended content.

This study establishes that the $\pi$-calculus is behaviourally complete, a result that follows from proving its transition system is orbit-finitely executable. The proof strategy involves demonstrating that every configuration reachable via a finite sequence of transitions admits an associated element of a single, canonically defined set of representative configurations within that system.

We introduce a circular adjacency framework for ordered binary trees, demonstrating that it possesses a Hamming code property regarding this adjacency. Furthermore, we show that this circular graph comprises both a Harpwood-Harper graph and a circulant graph, offering a straightforward method to calculate its diameter. Finally, we develop a circular isometry within this framework that corresponds to a depth-first traversal of the binary trees.

The sPHENIX experiment at Brookhaven National Lab's Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) is designed to investigate the properties of the hot, dense medium formed during high-energy nuclear collisions. It aims to analyze the momentum spectra of charged hadrons and the jet structures resulting from partons traversing this medium. A primary challenge for sPHENIX is the significant background from minimum-bias events and inelastic collisions, which can mimic jets. To address this, the experiment utilizes a sophisticated multi-layer tracking system, currently under construction, which will provide precise charged particle reconstruction and vertexing. This paper details the integration of the digital data from the upcoming 2020 detector upgrade into the sPHENIX track reconstruction software.

This paper introduces a generalized approach for calculating jump terms in space-time finite element methods, accommodating arbitrary degrees of temporal polynomial interpolation. By deriving the jump terms through the method of residues, we establish a unified framework that extends previous work relying on linear temporal interpolation. We demonstrate this technique using both the diagonal and collocation versions of the space-time FEM to solve parabolic partial differential equations. Furthermore, we provide numerical examples to validate the theoretical findings.

A signed graph consists of edges labeled as either positive or negative. It is defined as balanced when the product of the signs for every balanced bipartite subgraph is positive. This work introduces circular flows for uni-directed signed graphs, representing a variant of the circular flow problem. We demonstrate that the existence of a 4/3-circulating flow in such a graph is equivalent to the graph being balanced, and we provide a constructive algorithm to generate these flows when they exist.

The Subset Sum problem involves determining whether a specified target can be formed by summing a subset of a given collection of numbers. While the deterministic fastest known solution for the general case, running in $O(2^{0.2889n})$ time, was established by the author of this text, the current study introduces a faster algorithm achieving a runtime of $O(2^{0.2936n})$. This improvement is achieved by applying the Fast Fourier Transform to the method originally proposed by the author of this paper.

We present a catalog of 1,000 M-dwarf bursts identified by the All-Sky Automated Survey for Supernovae (ASAS-SN). These events were selected based on a rapid rise in brightness followed by a gradual decline, with peak-to-trough magnitude differences exceeding 1.5 magnitudes. The catalog includes the source's right ascension, declination, peak magnitude, and the time elapsed between the start and peak of the burst. We also provide the burst's duration, the time elapsed between the start and end of the burst, the source's color, and the source's magnitude.
