This study introduces a novel analytical framework for modeling the stochastic boundary of a random walk, a model widely used to describe the retreat of coastlines and ice sheet margins. Our approach is founded on the principle that the boundary's movement is triggered by the first particle exiting the bulk, a mechanism that becomes active only after sufficient accumulated bulk material exists to influence the boundary. We demonstrate that this "first departure" effect significantly alters the boundary's statistical characteristics, particularly at early stages of recession, causing the mean retreat rate to be orders of magnitude faster than predictions based on standard diffusion theory. Furthermore, we show that the probability distribution of these first departures is non-exponential and that the boundary's evolution is highly sensitive to the bulk's initial configuration.

We introduce a novel category of hyperbolic hyperbolic L-space links, termed $L^+$-links, and establish an algorithm to compute their associated L-space scalar polynomial $L(\lambda)$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the degree sequence of the $L(\lambda)$ for these $L^+$-links is determined by the lengths of their Seifert circles. This result allows us to extend several known findings regarding L-space knots to the domain of L-space links.

We introduce a new kinetic framework for relativistic hydrodynamics that extends the ideal model by incorporating a non-uniform entropy density. This approach is derived from a collisionless Boltzmann equation featuring a non-hydrodynamic background, which is subsequently projected onto the hydrodynamic manifold via a newly defined collisionless Boltzmann operator. This operator ensures the conservation of energy and momentum while maintaining the adiabatic nature of the resulting fluid evolution. We demonstrate that this framework possesses a specific Poisson structure, establishing a clear connection to ideal hydrodynamics. Furthermore, we analyze the behavior of entropy production and the associated entropy current, which are both linked to the gradients of this entropy density.

This study introduces a novel ensemble methodology designed to enhance the robustness of endoscopic video-based surgical artifact detection. The approach integrates a state-of-the-art object detector with a newly developed artifact detection algorithm. We evaluated the system using data from 100 minimally invasive cholecystectomy procedures, comparing its performance against a baseline method that relies solely on the object detector. Results indicate that the proposed ensemble significantly boosts the robustness of the baseline, achieving an average improvement of 10.4% in the F1-score.

Identifying classes and methods in source code is a foundational task for various software engineering activities, including refactoring, code analysis, and visualization. This paper examines the challenges of modeling identifiers using grammars, specifically focusing on two issues: the inherent difficulty of modeling these identifiers and the necessity of defining semantic constraints. We introduce a general framework for generating and defining grammars for identifiers, which is then applied to create a specific grammar for Java identifiers. This approach is further utilized to develop a grammar for identifiers in the Visual Studio Code extension marketplace.

We introduce a module, $M$, over the quantum shuffle algebra associated with affine $\mathfrak{sl}_2$, which is isomorphic to the affine vertex operator algebra $V_k^\mathfrak{sl}_2$ at the critical level $k=-2$ (or the specified critical value context). The module $M$ is established as an irreducible, infinite-dimensional representation of the quantum shuffle algebra that is both cyclic and generated by a single vector. Furthermore, we demonstrate that $M$ possesses the structure of a highest weight module for the affine Lie algebra $\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}}_2$, carrying a specific critical central value.

Grain growth is a fundamental process in materials science, yet its mechanisms remain incompletely understood. While traditional models rely on the assumption that grain boundaries move at a constant velocity, this study utilizes a data-driven approach to investigate the kinetics of grain growth in duplex and triplex systems. By analyzing extensive datasets from a two-dimensional grain growth model, we demonstrate that the velocity of a grain boundary is not constant but instead varies with the local curvature of that boundary. Furthermore, we show that triplex systems exhibit a more complex growth behavior compared to duplex ones. These findings offer critical insights for enhancing the accuracy of grain growth models and advancing the development of new materials.

This study introduces a benchmark and evaluation framework for 3D human pose and shape estimation. We examine the impact of various factors on 3D human pose and shape estimation, including pose and shape complexity, occlusion, and the 3D training data. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of existing methods and highlight promising future research directions.

We investigate the superconducting properties of a two-dimensional lattice system featuring sparse sites with on-site attractive interactions and off-site repulsive interactions between electrons. By employing the variational method, we derive the ground state energy and order parameter for a system with a low density of sites. Our analysis reveals that superconductivity can emerge even when repulsive forces between sites are substantial, provided the on-site attractive energy is sufficiently strong.

This study introduces a universal methodology for aligning the complete framework of scalar leptoquarks with experimental data. The approach integrates the latest theoretical and experimental advancements, including the most recent LHC findings, the full set of lepton flavor-violating constraints, and the latest global fits for quark mixing parameters. By employing a comprehensive set of Wilson coefficients, the method accounts for all observable effects arising from the scalar leptoquark model. We demonstrate that this strategy is both exhaustive and consistent, and we provide the corresponding matching code.

This approach is applied to the analysis of the category science, a two-dimensional dataset comprising 1,707 entries. Our findings reveal that the data contains a distinct pattern, which we term the "category science," with a correlation coefficient of 0.95.

This study introduces a novel optimal terminal sliding-mode control (OTSMC) strategy designed for the precise regulation of second-order dynamic systems. By integrating optimal control principles with terminal sliding-mode control, the proposed approach ensures that the system state converges to the desired reference in a finite time while eliminating chattering. Furthermore, the paper outlines a systematic method for determining the control parameters, including the sliding surface coefficients and the terminal exponent, and provides a rigorous stability analysis. Simulation results demonstrate that the OTSMC scheme achieves superior performance compared to existing terminal sliding-mode and optimal control techniques.

Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) are essential for modern energy storage and power systems, yet their internal architecture remains largely inaccessible to direct observation. This study introduces a non-destructive, quantitative method to characterize the layered structure within LIBs by utilizing resonance frequencies generated by a non-contact ultrasonic transducer. By analyzing the acoustic response, we successfully identified distinct resonances corresponding to specific layers, including the separator, electrodes, and current collectors. Furthermore, we established a quantitative relationship between the acoustic resonance frequencies and the thickness of these individual components. This approach offers a robust means to assess the internal layer architecture of LIBs, facilitating the development of more efficient and reliable energy storage solutions.

This paper introduces a discrete-time flatness-based control method for gantry cranes. The approach involves deriving a discrete-time model of the system and applying flatness theory to this model, followed by the development of a tracking control algorithm designed to follow desired trajectories. The study evaluates the method's effectiveness through numerical simulations, comparing its performance against a traditional PID controller.

Image captioning involves generating textual descriptions for input images. While current state-of-the-art methods rely on pre-trained vision encoders to extract visual features, these models often produce noisy information that hinders the generation of accurate captions. To address this, we introduce Cooperative Distillation, a novel framework designed to mitigate such noise. This approach leverages the complementary strengths of two distinct pre-trained vision encoders to produce robust visual representations. Specifically, we utilize a "teacher" encoder to filter out noise from the "student" encoder's output through a collaborative distillation process. This is achieved by training the student to match the teacher's feature distribution, while simultaneously employing a feature-level distillation loss to align their representations. Additionally, we incorporate a regularization term to ensure the student encoder learns to generate high-quality captions directly. Comprehensive experiments on the MS-COCO dataset demonstrate that our method surpasses existing techniques, yielding significant performance improvements.

A collection of binary strings is defined as well-linked if there exists a network connecting all string vertices such that every cut-vertex avoids being a cut-vertex for any pair of string vertices. This paper addresses the problem of determining the maximum size of a well-linked set given $n$ strings of a fixed length $p$. We establish that for sufficiently large $p$, every well-linked set of strings can be transformed into a well-linked set of Hamming distance 1. Leveraging this finding, we derive a lower bound for the maximum size of a well-linked set of strings of a fixed length $p$ and $n$ strings. Additionally, we provide an upper bound for a well-linked set of strings of a fixed length $p$ and $n$ strings. Finally, we demonstrate that these bounds coincide when $p$ is sufficiently large.

Ehresmann monoids are defined as algebraic structures that model the algebraic properties inherent in directed acyclic graphs. This paper establishes a specific definition for ordered Ehresmann monoids and investigates their fundamental characteristics. Furthermore, we demonstrate a natural correspondence linking these monoids to ordered inverse semigroups, thereby transferring the corresponding theory of ordered inverse semigroups to the context of Ehresmann monoids.

Self-attention mechanisms have become a cornerstone of modern language models, with their performance heavily dependent on architectural design choices. This study investigates how model depth and width influence self-attention performance. We demonstrate that shallow architectures with a large vocabulary size (high width) are superior for learning the global context of input sequences, whereas deeper models with a narrower width excel at capturing local context. Furthermore, we find that increasing model width enhances the generalization capabilities of self-attention, a trend that holds true regardless of whether the model is shallow or deep.

This study details the synthesis of BiFeO$_{3}$ nanoparticles (BNOs) using a sol-gel method at low temperatures, followed by a comparative analysis of their structural, morphological, and magnetic characteristics. The resulting BNOs exhibit a hexagonal morphology with a particle size of approximately 10 nm. Notably, the material displays a room-temperature saturation magnetization of 1.1 emu/g, a value significantly higher than those reported for BNOs produced via other methods. Furthermore, the material demonstrates robust photocatalytic activity, evidenced by a 90% degradation of Rhodamine B after 120 minutes of irradiation and a hydrogen evolution rate of 1.1 mmol h$^{-1}$ g$^{-1}$ in a water splitting application. These findings underscore the potential of BNOs as a highly effective multifunctional material for spintronics and environmental remediation.

This study examines the chiral symmetry breaking pattern within a toy $\mathrm{SU}(6)$ gauge theory featuring a single generation of fermions, specifically a doublet of $\tau$ leptons and a bottom quark. We analyze the resulting spectrum of composite states, focusing on the masses of the pseudo-Goldstone bosons, the bottom quark, and the tau lepton. By employing a model-independent approach, we determine the weights of the bottom quark and tau lepton in the composite state spectrum. We demonstrate that the predicted weights for the bottom quark and tau lepton align with experimental observations, thereby validating the model's viability.

This study introduces a novel 3D reconstruction challenge focused on generic objects held in human hands. We begin by assembling a substantial 3D dataset of such grasped items, featuring 1,000 objects captured from 10,000 distinct viewpoints. To address the inherent difficulties of this problem, we propose a hybrid approach combining 2D and 3D deep learning. This method employs a 2D convolutional neural network to detect the object and its grasp configuration within an image, followed by a 3D convolutional neural network that utilizes this 2D output to predict the object's 3D shape. Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques.

The Ca-K index serves as a primary indicator of chromospheric activity in the Sun, derived from the absorption depth of the K line at 393.3 nm within the Ca II K spectrum. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the Ca-K index over the past century, utilizing a unique set of equal-contrast images captured by the Kodaikanal Observatory. We detail the data reduction process, which includes flat-fielding, normalization, and contrast adjustment, and evaluate the resulting index's reliability. Furthermore, we examine the long-term variability of the Ca-K index and its correlation with other solar activity metrics, including the Wolf number, F10.7 cm flux, and the Mg II 303 nm index.

This study reports the first observation of the $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decay, utilizing LHCb proton-proton collision data collected at $\sqrt{s}=7$ and $8$ TeV with an integrated luminosity of $9.0$ fb$^{-1}$. The analysis employs a binned maximum likelihood fit to the proton-muon invariant mass distribution to determine the branching fraction, which is measured as $\mathcal{B}(\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-) = (1.71 \pm 0.14_{\rm stat} \pm 0.14_{\rm syst}) \times 10^{-3}$. This result is consistent with the Standard Model prediction, which anticipates a branching fraction of $(1.71 \pm 0.14_{\rm stat} \pm 0.14_{\rm syst}) \times 10^{-3}$.

Test assessment is a critical component of VLSI design, aiming to identify faults in a chip by applying test patterns and analyzing the resulting outputs. While existing methods typically focus on generating these patterns, they often overlook the computational complexity of the evaluation phase. This paper introduces a novel distributed methodology that leverages symbolic computation to enhance both efficiency and fault coverage. The approach utilizes a test-depth-based partitioning strategy to divide the circuit into smaller, manageable sub-circuits, which are then assessed independently. This technique is particularly effective for large-scale designs, as it significantly reduces the memory and computational resources required for both assessment and pattern generation. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the proposed method achieves superior fault coverage compared to traditional techniques.

This study investigates the relaxation of magnetic nanoparticle chains formed in arranged assembly. We demonstrate that the relaxation of these chains is governed by the interplay between dipolar forces and steric hindrance. Furthermore, we establish that the relaxation kinetics are non-exponential and follow a power-law distribution of activation energies. Finally, we conclude that the Arranged Assembly technique is essential for comprehensively understanding the relaxation dynamics of dipole-coupled systems.

Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a promising approach for training machine learning models across distributed devices, yet its practical adoption faces significant hurdles. A primary obstacle is the reliance on a central server, which creates privacy risks and scalability constraints. Furthermore, FL protocols typically depend on a transitive trust model, which is often unrealistic in real-world scenarios where not all participants can be trusted. To address these limitations, we introduce a decentralized FL framework designed for single-sided trust communities. This system leverages existing trans-community trust relationships to establish a trustworthy, decentralized architecture. We propose a novel, serverless protocol that enables agents to train models collaboratively while safeguarding their data privacy. Additionally, we develop a lightweight mechanism to verify the integrity of the federated aggregation process. Experimental results indicate that our approach achieves performance comparable to centralized FL systems while offering superior scalability and adaptability.

This study introduces a sequential text categorization framework utilizing Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN). The method employs a hybrid architecture that integrates RNNs for modeling text sequences with CNNs for extracting features from individual text units. Experimental results indicate that this approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in sequential text classification tasks.

This study presents an analytical formulation for the telecentric Fabry-P\'erot etalon, treating the device as a system of two parallel, partially reflective surfaces. We establish a comprehensive analytical framework for the etalon's transmission and reflection coefficients, applicable to both normal incidence and oblique angles. This approach accommodates arbitrary spatially varying phase shifts and complex amplitude ratios at the surfaces, thereby enabling the analysis of etalons equipped with complex internal components. Furthermore, we derive a general formula for the etalon's finesse, which is subsequently applied to examine the characteristics of etalons incorporating beam splitters and spatial light modulators.

We investigate the problem of Consistent Matching (CM), which involves identifying a set of vertex-disjoint paths and cycles in a directed graph $G$ that connect a specified collection of ordered pairs. This research establishes that determining such matchings is NP-complete, even when the graph $G$ is restricted to being a planar grid. We further demonstrate that the problem remains NP-complete if the graph $G$ is a planar grid and the given pairs are restricted to having a maximum $y$-coordinate difference of 1. Conversely, we also prove that the problem is solvable in polynomial time when the input graph $G$ is a planar grid and the given pairs exhibit a constant maximum $y$-coordinate difference.

Chiplets represent a novel approach to integrated circuit design, offering a flexible and cost-effective method for creating complex systems. This work outlines a design framework for chiplets that enables the reuse of hardware components across diverse applications. We introduce a hardware description language (HDL) for chiplets that supports modular, hierarchical design, alongside a runtime architecture for the dynamic composition of these chiplets into larger systems. Furthermore, we present a codelet framework that facilitates the development of chiplet applications in a functional style, featuring a high-level language for concurrent, distributed computations and a compiler that compiles this code into executable sequences for individual codelets. These codelets can be efficiently dispatched to their target chiplets by the runtime system. We demonstrate the practical utility of this methodology through a series of case studies.

Mixture cure models are widely utilized in survival analysis to address data where a subset of the population remains uncured. While recent methodological advancements have largely focused on semiparametric versions of these models, this paper introduces a new semiparametric cure model designed for right-censored survival settings. The proposed approach employs a semiparametric structure that combines a finite mixture distribution for the cured population with a Cox proportional hazards framework for the uncured. We develop a presmoothing technique to estimate the cure model parameters, which involves an initial step of smoothing the estimated non-cured hazard function before applying a Newton-Raphson algorithm to refine the final estimates. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the resulting estimators are consistent and asymptotically normal. Furthermore, a simulation study was conducted to evaluate the finite-sample performance of the proposed method. Finally, the application of this new model is illustrated using two real-world datasets.

We establish that the dimensions of large-scale measure spaces on graphs, as defined by nonlocal measures, are governed by the measures' decay rates. Specifically, we demonstrate that for graphs exhibiting polynomial growth, the dimension relative to the $\ell^1$ measure diminishes asymptotically with the inverse of the growth's exponent. Furthermore, we prove that the same holds for graphs with polynomial measure Laplacians when utilizing the $\ell^2$ measure.

The rise of specialized hardware accelerators has spurred the development of in-memory computing (IMC) architectures designed to overcome the von Neumann bottleneck. However, this architectural shift introduces new vulnerabilities, including side-channel attacks. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of such attacks targeting IMC architectures. We first examine the physical side-channel leakage inherent in these systems, followed by the identification of various attack vectors. We then detail the specific countermeasures proposed to defend against these threats. Finally, we outline a comprehensive defense strategy to safeguard IMC systems from side-channel exploits.

We introduce a polarized kernel designed to capture the nonperturbant dynamics of parton polarization within hadrons. This kernel is defined through the light-cone correlation function of two twist-3, spin-1 quark-antiquark operators, where one includes a gamma-matrix gamma5 insertion. We establish a direct connection between this kernel and various measurable polarization observables, such as single-spin asymmetries in semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering and single-spin dependent Drell-Yan production. Additionally, we derive a factorization theorem applicable to these observables, which expresses them as a convolution of this new kernel with perturbatively calculable parton distributions.

This study introduces a self-supervised deep learning approach for eliminating blind spot noise from seismic data. The method employs a convolutional autoencoder where the convolutional decoder mirrors the encoder's architecture, with blind spot masking applied to the decoder's input. The encoder learns to reconstruct the masked input using a loss function that penalizes differences between its output and the decoder's reconstruction. This strategy was tested on synthetic data, where the autoencoder successfully removed the blind spot noise. The method was further applied to real-world data, where it achieved a significant reduction in the target blind spot noise.

This study examines the charge asymmetry arising from real photon emission in lepton and antilepton- nucleon elastic scattering, focusing on the impact of one-loop radiative corrections. We derive the leading-order analytical expressions for radiative contributions to scattering amplitudes, accounting for both internal and external leg corrections. Our findings indicate that radiative effects are most pronounced at high momentum transfers and low lepton energies, yielding a charge asymmetry of approximately 10% in the extreme kinematic limit. Furthermore, we demonstrate that radiative effects are intrinsically linked to the finite nucleon mass, a factor that plays a crucial role in determining the magnitude of charge asymmetry.

The spin-orbit-coupling-driven Mott semiconductor Sr$_2$IrO$_{4}$ exhibits a distinctive electronic structure characterized by a narrow, spin-polaron-like band. This study utilizes scanning tunneling spectroscopy to investigate the dispersion of this band, revealing a pronounced dependence on tunneling direction. This anisotropy is attributed to spin-polaron formation, which arises from the interaction between localized electrons and spin fluctuations within the lattice.

This study introduces a method for examining causal mediation effects involving continuous treatment and outcome variables, even when the mediator is affected by the treatment confoundingly. The approach is grounded in multiply robust frameworks, ensuring valid results if at least one model among four specific structures—mediating mechanisms, treatment assignment, or overall effects—is correctly specified. We develop a double machine learning algorithm to estimate the average causal mediation effect, utilizing cross-fitting and sample splitting to mitigate bias arising from the application of machine learning models. Furthermore, we establish theoretical guarantees regarding the estimator's asymptotic normality and root-n consistency. Finally, we validate the method's performance through simulations and apply it to real-world data.

This special issue, which is now complete, features contributions from 21 authors across 22 papers detailing the current state of the field, technical hurdles, and future prospects regarding the development of the starshade. The articles are organized into four sections: an introductory overview of the starshade concept, foundational aspects of its design, optical engineering, and mission architecture. The final section includes a guest editorial that synthesizes the issue's content and outlines a dialogue on the future trajectory of the starshade.

This study introduces Robin, an online collection of suicidal content gathered from 2014 to 2019 across 11 distinct platforms, including social media, blogs, and forums. The dataset comprises 1,000,000 texts, with 100,000 manually annotated for suicide-related content, covering 10 different languages. The authors detail the data gathering and annotation processes, evaluate various suicide detection models, and release the dataset publicly to advance research in suicide prevention.

This study examines the difference equation $x_{n+1}=ax^\alpha_{n}+bx^\alpha_{n-1}$, where $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$, $0<\alpha\leq 2$, and $n$ is a non-negative integer with initial values $x_0, x_1\in\mathbb{R}$. We establish the global existence of solutions and analyze the convergence of the zero equilibrium point. Furthermore, we prove that the zero point is globally asymptotically stable whenever $|a|<1$ and $|b|<1$. In addition, we demonstrate that the global attractivity of the zero point is achieved under the conditions $|a|<1$ and $|b|<1$ when $\alpha=2$. Finally, we explore the global behavior of the zero point for cases where $|a|\geq 1$ or $|b|\geq 1$.

This study examines a specific model of electrodynamics derived from aggregating multiple Born-Infeld-type theories, which are characterized by distinct parameters. We analyze the properties of charged black holes within this framework, demonstrating that the horizon area and ADM mass are linked by a Bekenstein-Hawking relation. Furthermore, we establish that these charged black holes satisfy the first law of black hole thermodynamics.

This work introduces the concept of a Sidon collection, defined as a family of linear forms where every product of a given degree appears at most once. We establish an upper bound for the cardinality of such collections, which is determined by the dimension of the ambient space. Leveraging this result, we demonstrate that any set containing a sufficiently large number of elements will include nontrivial solutions to equations of the shape $\sum_{i=1}^d \pm f_i=0$, provided the linear forms $f_i$ originate from a Sidon collection.

We examine the finite-temperature magnetic properties of the spin-1/2 XY chain, specifically focusing on the magnetic susceptibility and the geometric phase. Our findings indicate that the susceptibility exhibits a peak that scales with temperature, a behavior that persists across various external magnetic fields. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the susceptibility can be expressed as a function of the scaled temperature and the scaled magnetic field. Additionally, we establish that the susceptibility at the zero-frequency limit corresponds to the geometric phase.

This study investigates the phase transition of a paramagnetic system into a ferromagnetic state within a 2D Ising model, utilizing Monte Carlo simulations to analyze the impact of initial temperatures on the transition process. The findings indicate that systems initialized at higher temperatures transition to the ferromagnetic state more rapidly than those started at lower temperatures. This outcome contradicts the intuitive expectation that lower initial temperatures facilitate a quicker transition. The research attributes this counterintuitive behavior to the fact that high initial temperatures accelerate the formation of spin clusters, which serve as the fundamental building blocks for the eventual ferromagnetic state.

We examine the localization behavior of pairs within one-dimensional quasicrystals that exhibit power-law hopping ratios. Specifically, this study addresses the pair hopping model defined by the Hamiltonian $H = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (t_1 c^\dagger_{n+1} c_n + t_2 c^\dagger_{n+1} c_{n+1} + h.c.)$, where the hopping amplitudes $t_1$ and $t_2$ adhere to a power-law relationship. We demonstrate that when the ratio of these amplitudes is irrational, all eigenstates of the model are localized. Furthermore, this work extends the methodology introduced by Damanik and Tcheremchantsev in their 2016 paper on localization for the pair model with constant amplitudes.

The field of Natural Language Processing (NLP) has recently advanced significantly, particularly in the realm of conversational agents. These systems are now capable of engaging in fluent, open-ended dialogues with humans, yet they still face substantial hurdles in handling the complexities of real-world interactions. This paper examines a specific subset of these challenges: task-oriented dialogue systems (TODS). Unlike general conversational agents, TODS are designed to execute particular tasks, such as booking flights or ordering food. We provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of TODS research, highlighting key challenges and potential solutions. Furthermore, we introduce a novel framework for analyzing these systems, which we apply to discuss the latest advancements in multilingual TODS. We conclude by outlining future research directions and open questions within this domain.

We introduce a probabilistic framework designed to identify differentially spliced transcripts and pinpoint specific splicing events within differential splicing studies. This approach models splicing event isoform usage as a multinomial distribution, where the likelihood parameters reflect the relative abundances of alternative isoforms. By utilizing a Bayesian formulation, we estimate these isoform usage parameters and their uncertainties for both control and experimental conditions. Subsequently, we calculate the probability of observing the measured data under the null hypothesis of no splicing differences to determine statistical significance. This method was applied to a dataset from a breast cancer study, revealing 1,066 significantly regulated transcripts. Our findings indicate that the majority of these transcripts exhibit regulation through a single splicing event, while the remaining ones are regulated by two or more events. Furthermore, we identified 1,606 alternative exons and 1,406 alternative splice sites that drive this differential regulation.

The escalating volume of data generated and processed daily has heightened the risk of data breaches, prompting governments worldwide to enact data protection laws. However, the intricate nature of these regulations, coupled with the technical complexity of implementing necessary safeguards, makes compliance a significant challenge for organizations. This study aims to investigate how organizations apply technical controls to meet data privacy mandates. Using a qualitative methodology, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 14 data protection officers from various sectors in Brazil. The findings reveal that organizations typically deploy a mix of technical measures to address regulatory requirements, with the specific combination varying based on the type of data handled. Furthermore, we identified a critical gap: although organizations implement controls to protect data in use and at rest, they largely fail to address data in transit. The study concludes by offering practical recommendations for organizations seeking to navigate the complexities of data protection law compliance.

We introduce a new method for analyzing multiparticle azimuthal angular correlations in proton-nucleus collisions, which relies on the Fourier decomposition of the azimuthal angles of particles within each event. This approach yields coefficients that are independent of event multiplicity, and we demonstrate that these coefficients can be derived from the Fourier coefficients of the azimuthal angle distribution across the entire event system. Furthermore, we establish a direct relationship between the newly defined coefficients and those of the Fourier expansion of the $n$-particle azimuthal cumulant distribution, revealing that the former can be expressed as a function of the latter. Finally, we apply this technique to proton-nucleus collisions at the Large Hadron Collider, specifically examining the four- and five-particle correlation coefficients.

This study investigates the production of light nuclei in Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=3$ GeV, utilizing a novel approach to analyze the coalescence mechanism. By examining the dependence of the light nuclei-to-hadron ratios on the transverse momentum ($p_{T}$) of the hadrons, the analysis reveals that the $p_{T}$ dependence of the ratios for $d$, $t$, $^3$He, and $^4$He is consistent with a single coalescence source. However, the ratios for $^3$H and $^4$He deviate from this pattern, indicating the presence of an additional source for their production. Furthermore, the study finds that the $d$-$t$ ratio is nearly independent of $p_{T}$, suggesting that deuterons and tritons originate from the same source but are produced through distinct reaction mechanisms.

The habitability of rocky exoplanets is heavily influenced by their surrounding environments, which are in turn governed by the host star's characteristics and the planet's orbital parameters. This study examines the environmental conditions of 1,000 rocky exoplanets, utilizing a dataset of 2,000 confirmed rocky candidates identified by the Kepler mission. We analyze the stellar properties of these systems, including the host star's mass, radius, and effective temperature, alongside the planet's orbital distance and orbital period. Additionally, we calculate the bolometric flux received by each planet and determine the host star's luminosity. We also assess the planet's equilibrium temperature, the host star's apparent magnitude, and the planet's albedo. Our results indicate that the majority of these rocky worlds orbit M-type stars, with a significant portion of the host stars being M-dwarfs. A graph $G$ is defined as $k$-dispersible when its vertex set can be partitioned into $k$ independent sets and one cluster of vertices with a maximum degree of $k-1$. This study examines circulant graphs $C_n(\{1,2, \dots, k\})$ to establish sufficient conditions ensuring $k$-dispersibility. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for any integer $k \geq 2$, circulant graphs $C_n(\{1,2, \dots, k\})$ are $k$-dispersible whenever $n \geq 2k^2 - 2k$.

This study introduces a novel approach to computing the inverse of a matrix, building upon a recent higher-order technique originally proposed by the authors. The matrix inverse is essential for numerous applications, including the solution of linear systems, least squares problems, and statistical analysis. While higher-order methods offer a significant advantage by calculating multiple inverse updates through a single matrix multiplication, they are typically restricted to small matrices due to the high computational cost of calculating the adjugate and trace. To overcome this limitation, we present a new algorithm that accelerates these operations by leveraging GPU parallelization. Our approach achieves a speedup of 100x compared to sequential processing on a standard CPU. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the GPU implementation is 100 times faster than the sequential CPU implementation.

We investigate primordial fluctuations within the framework of ultra-slow-roll (USR) inflation, specifically accounting for back reaction effects. By employing the Einstein equations for the Einstein-Brans-Dicke model, we derive the power spectrum of these fluctuations. Our findings indicate that the power spectrum exhibits a significantly amplified super-horizon amplitude compared to standard slow-roll inflation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the super-horizon spectrum remains nearly scale-invariant, a result that holds true even when the back reaction effects are included.

In clinical trials, survival analysis is a standard method for evaluating outcomes, yet it is frequently employed incorrectly. This paper introduces a novel approach to survival analysis that utilizes a case-based framework. By organizing data into a two-by-two table that stratifies subjects based on treatment assignment and event occurrence, this method offers a fresh perspective on survival data interpretation. We demonstrate that the statistical tests used in this approach are mathematically equivalent to those in traditional survival analysis, yet they provide a more intuitive understanding of event rates. Furthermore, the method's flexibility allows it to be adapted for censored data, time-dependent covariates, and competing risks.

We examine the potential for computing multi-loop, multi-scale Feynman integrals with high precision required for precision physics. This investigation utilizes a six-point massless scalar integral featuring two non-propagating non-zero virtual masses, which serves as a test case for one of the most demanding scenarios. We detail a methodology to evaluate this integral with exceptional accuracy, even when faced with extreme parameter configurations. Furthermore, we explore the implications of this study for precision physics and identify several outstanding challenges.

This study evaluates the performance of two distinct data management strategies for high-performance computing (HPC) systems: the conventional file system approach utilizing Lustre, and an emerging object storage approach based on DAOS. The research focuses on the impact of these approaches on data access latency and throughput, specifically examining the effects of varying data sizes and concurrency levels. The analysis covers a range of scenarios, including single-node operations with sequential and random access, as well as multi-node operations with sequential and random access. The results indicate that the object storage model consistently outperforms the file system model in terms of latency and throughput, with the advantage widening as data size increases.

The growing adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) is anticipated to significantly boost the demand for public EV charging stations. This paper introduces an online access control mechanism designed for EV drivers seeking charging services at public infrastructure. The system operates by issuing time-limited tokens that grant a specific number of charging sessions. These tokens are sold in advance through an online platform, and users redeem them via a mobile application upon arrival at the parking facility. The study presents a charging queueing model that incorporates the token-based access scheme and analyzes the system's performance using the mean value analysis method. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed mechanism effectively manages congestion and minimizes the average waiting time for EV drivers.

A linear code defined over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ with parameters $[n,k,d]$ is termed a linearly independent code (LCD code) when its generator matrix possesses full rank. This study examines the existence and construction of such codes over $\mathbb{F}_q$. Specifically, we demonstrate that for any finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ and any positive integer $n$, an LCD code with parameters $[n,k,d]$ exists provided that $d \le \min\{n-k+1,2k-1\}$. Furthermore, we present the existence and creation of these codes over $\mathbb{F}_q$ under the constraints $d \le \min\{n-k+1,3k-2\}$ and $d \le \min\{n-k+1,\frac{3}{2}k\}$, respectively.

We present a comprehensive framework for computing loop amplitudes in effective field theories containing massless spin-2 fields, which notably encompasses Einstein gravity. This formalism relies on a "unitarity cut" program that extends the on-shell method to loop level, treating gravitons as on-shell particles within cut diagrams. We establish the unitarity method as a potent instrument for deriving new results regarding multi-graviton scattering at high energies and low momentum transfers. Specifically, we demonstrate that traditional quantum corrections to Einstein gravity are finite and calculable using standard perturbation theory. Furthermore, we identify the precise counterterms required to renormalize Einstein gravity coupled to matter, thereby confirming its renormalizability within the effective field theory paradigm.

Achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 necessitates a massive transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy, yet this shift often competes with other land uses, creating a complex trade-off between land availability and decarbonization goals. This study examines the interplay between land use and the transformation of the U.S. Western power grid, specifically focusing on the American West. We developed a detailed land-use model that integrates land-use types, soil quality, and water requirements to simulate the conversion of fossil-fuel plants into solar and wind generation. Our results indicate that the U.S. West possesses sufficient land resources to meet 100% of the region's electricity demand through renewables. However, this outcome relies on significant changes in land use, including the conversion of 1.2 million hectares of cropland and 1.6 million hectares of pasture into solar and wind farms. Furthermore, we observe that the transition from fossil fuels to renewables can be achieved with a minimal reduction in the region's total biomass carbon stock.

Cluster-randomized trials (CRFs) are frequently employed to evaluate vaccine efficacy, yet the estimands they target often diverge from those defined in conventional randomized controlled trials (RCTs). In standard RCTs, estimands typically isolate the average causal effect of an individual vaccine dose on a person's health outcomes. Conversely, in cluster-randomized vaccine trials, estimands are often defined to measure the average causal effect of vaccinating an entire population on aggregate health outcomes. This distinction arises because cluster-randomized designs are uniquely suited to capture indirect effects—specifically, the impact of vaccination on unvaccinated individuals through herd immunity. Consequently, the estimands selected for cluster-randomized vaccine trials necessitate distinct statistical methods and lead to conclusions that differ fundamentally from those drawn in standard RCTs.

The study of spectral graph theory has gained significant attention in recent years, with the Laplacian spectrum of various graph types being extensively examined. This paper focuses on fractal Mobius octagonal networks, denoted as $M\mathcal{O}_n$, and analyzes their normalized Laplacian spectrum, denoted as $\Lambda(M\mathcal{O}_n)$. We derive the spectrum for these networks and utilize the resulting eigenvalues to determine key topological invariants, including the algebraic connectivity, vertex connectivity, and the first non-zero eigenvalue of the Rayleigh quotient. Furthermore, we calculate the asymptotic behavior of the eigenvalue distribution for $L(M\mathcal{O}_n)$ and the multiplicity count of eigenvalues within $L(M\mathcal{O}_n)$.

We examine distributed contextual linear bandits, where multiple agents must select actions within a shared environment to maximize cumulative rewards. This research addresses a scenario in which agents possess distinct, non-identifiable reward distributions, preventing them from revealing their local reward functions to one another. We introduce a decentralized algorithm that achieves a regret bound matching the optimal rate achievable by a fully connected central system. The proposed method relies on a lightweight exchange of only the observed rewards and context vectors between agents, eliminating the need to share local reward functions.

Synthetic data serves as a valuable resource for research and development, particularly in healthcare, where it enables the sharing of sensitive information while preserving patient privacy. This paper introduces a new dataset derived from real-world electronic health records (EHRs) of patients with cystic fibrosis. The dataset comprises 1,000 anonymized records, each containing up to 10 years of longitudinal data. These records include patient demographics, clinical notes, and detailed information on medications, procedures, and laboratory tests. To support the research community, we have made this dataset publicly available.

This study examines the resonance structure within the $D^0 \to K^\mp \pi^\pm \pi^\pm \pi^\mp$ decay modes. Utilizing a sample of $3.0 \, \text{fb}^{-1}$ of $pp$ collision data collected by the LHCb experiment at center-of-mass energies of $\sqrt{s} = 7$ and $8 \, \text{TeV}$, the analysis identifies three distinct decay channels: $D^0 \to D_s^- K^+ \to K_s^0 \pi^\pm K^\mp$ and $D^0 \to D_s^\mp K^\pm \to K_s^0 \pi^\pm K^\mp$. The $D_s^-$ intermediate state is reconstructed via the $K_s^0 \pi^\mp$ final state, where the $K_s^0$ meson is defined as a pair of oppositely charged pions. The observed mass distributions for the $D_s^-$ and $\bar{D_s}^\mp$ mesons align with previously established values. Furthermore, the branching fraction ratio between the two modes is determined to be $0.81 \pm 0.08 \, (\text{stat}) \, ^{+0.09}_{-0.08} \, (\text{syst})$.

Novelpy is a Python package designed to analyze bibliometric and patent datasets by calculating novelty and disruptiveness metrics for individual citations, patents, or authors. It employs a "neighborhood" methodology, determining these values based on the citation patterns of an item's related works. The package includes a suite of visualization tools and can be integrated into existing workflows via its command-line interface. The developers have demonstrated Novelpy's capabilities through various case studies, and the tool is freely available on GitHub.

This study introduces a method for achieving spatiotemporal control of laser intensity by leveraging cross-phase modulation (XPM) between two optical beams within a nonlinear crystal. The process involves overlapping a pump beam and a signal beam, where the intensity profile of the pump acts as a nonlinear grating that modulates the signal beam's phase. Subsequently, spatial Fourier transformation converts this phase modulation into intensity modulation. The resulting output intensity distribution is governed by the pump's profile, the beam overlap efficiency, and the degree of temporal walk-off. This technique offers a versatile approach for generating diverse intensity patterns in the signal beam, enabling applications in laser machining, holography, and optical imaging.

This paper investigates the feasibility of automating Olympic recurve bow shooting. While previous research has extensively covered the automation of other sports, recurve archery has not yet been addressed. We present a method to enable a robot to autonomously execute this complex sport, detailing a system comprising a specialized robot, a custom-built archery bow, and a computer vision setup. We demonstrate that the system can achieve a level of performance comparable to human competitors. Furthermore, we outline a high-level control strategy that enables the robot to shoot with high precision, and we provide empirical evidence confirming the system's ability to replicate human-level accuracy.

The primary challenge in recommender systems is the cold-start issue, which arises when new users or items lack sufficient historical data. While cross-domain recommendation offers a viable solution by leveraging data from related domains, it is frequently hindered by domain discrepancies that degrade model performance. To address this, we introduce Dual Metric Training (DMT), a framework designed to learn domain-invariant representations by utilizing two distinct metrics: a standard $L_2$ distance to capture the original data distribution and a cross-domain distance metric to measure similarity between domains. By jointly optimizing these objectives, our approach effectively mitigates the impact of domain shifts. Empirical evaluations across three real-world datasets demonstrate that DMT outperforms existing state-of-the-art cross-domain recommendation methods. Furthermore, our analysis confirms that the method maintains high efficiency, requiring only a single additional training epoch to achieve these gains.

We demonstrate that the modal mu-fragment can be characterized by asynchronous distributed machines, which are defined as extensions of the classical Muller machines that incorporate modal past operators and modal past modalities, all while maintaining the same structure and properties as described.

This study examines the thermal transfer within a two-dimensional complex plasma layer, specifically focusing on the interaction between a hot layer and a cold one. The analysis employs a two-temperature hydrodynamic model to determine the temperature distribution across the interface. Theoretical predictions are validated against experimental results obtained using a laser-induced plasma source, where the interface temperature was measured via a CCD camera. The findings indicate that the thermal transfer mechanism is governed by the thickness of the interface, which is determined by the initial velocity of the cold plasma.

This study examines the linear composition of unordered data vectors, a concept that encompasses the linear composition of multiset vectors, which serve as an extension of multiset representations. We introduce a novel algorithm capable of calculating the linear composition of two multiset vectors in O(n log n) time, where n represents the total count of elements across both vectors. Furthermore, we establish that the linear composition of two multiset vectors can be computed in O(n log k) time, where k denotes the maximum number of distinct elements found in either vector. We also present an algorithm for computing the linear composition of two general unordered data vectors in O(n log k) time, where k is the maximum number of distinct elements in the resulting composition vector. Finally, we demonstrate that the linear composition of two general unordered data vectors can be computed in O(n log k) time, where k represents the maximum number of distinct elements in the input vectors.

Fluoroscopy is a critical imaging modality for diagnosing and treating cardiovascular conditions, yet it exposes patients to substantial ionizing radiation. This study introduces a deep learning framework designed to lower radiation exposure by reducing the necessary fluoroscopy frame rate. The method utilizes a convolutional neural network (CNN) to interpolate missing frames from a sparse video sequence, thereby reconstructing a denser sequence with enhanced temporal resolution. The CNN architecture employs a dual-pathway design: one branch predicts the interpolated frames, while the other generates corresponding optical flow maps to capture motion dynamics. These optical flows are utilized to warp high-resolution frames, ensuring the CNN can effectively learn from sparse temporal data. Experimental results indicate that the proposed approach achieves a peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of 31.8 dB and a structural similarity index (SSIM) of 0.919, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods.

The proposed Future Circular Collider (FCC) project aims to install a 100 km circumference ring designed to host electron-positron collisions. The FCC is intended to comprise two distinct stages: the FCC-ee, which will operate as a high-luminosity electron-positron collider with center-of-mass energies ranging from 91 to 365 GeV, and the FCC-hh, a hadron collider targeting proton-proton center-of-mass energies between 77 and 132 TeV. This paper specifically examines the scientific potential of the FCC-ee for studying heavy-flavor hadrons.

We examine the impact of the dark sector on the relic density of dark matter, specifically within the leptophilic $U(1)_{X}$ framework. This scenario involves a dark matter candidate, $\chi$, interacting with Standard Model leptons via a $U(1)_{X}$ gauge boson, $Z'$. We analyze the constraints imposed by the relic density and the relic density's indirect detection limits, specifically focusing on the $U(1)_{\mu-\tau}$ model. We demonstrate that the dark sector can significantly alter the relic density, thereby relaxing the constraints imposed by indirect detection searches.

The ejection of hypervelocity stars (HVSs) from the Galactic center (GC) is primarily attributed to the Hills mechanism, which involves the tidal disruption of a binary system by a supermassive black hole (SMBH). This study investigates an alternative mechanism where a binary system undergoes secular evolution due to perturbations from an intermediate-mass black hole (IMBH) within the GC. This process can cause the binary to shrink and eventually result in the ejection of one component. We conducted numerical simulations of IMBH-induced secular evolution in binaries with varying mass ratios and initial eccentricities, utilizing the Hermite integrator. Our results indicate that the ejection velocity of the resulting star is highly dependent on the mass ratio, reaching a maximum of approximately 1000 km/s for equal-mass binaries. Furthermore, we determined that the ejection velocity decreases as the initial eccentricity increases. Finally, we calculated the ejection rate of stars via this secular mechanism, finding that it is highly sensitive to the IMH mass. For an IMH mass of 1000 M☉, the ejection rate is approximately 10⁻⁶ yr⁻¹, which is significantly lower than the rate predicted by the Hills mechanism.

This study examines the weak solutions of a specific singular stochastic differential equation (SDE) driven by multiplicative noise. The approach involves regularizing the original SDE through a perturbed variant, demonstrating that the weak solutions of this regularized system converge to a limiting object as the added disturbance vanishes. This limit is then established as the limiting equation's weak solution. The methodology draws inspiration from the concept of "regularization by noise," adapted here for the perturbation of the disturbance term.
We demonstrate that within the context of $PFA_{\omega_1}$, the definability of the nonstationary ideal on $\omega_1$ is equivalent to the existence of a global well-ordering.

Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success across numerous tasks, yet their inherent lack of generalization remains a significant hurdle. While prompt engineering has emerged as a simple and effective strategy for leveraging LLMs, it often necessitates extensive human effort to construct prompts and fine-tune models. To address this, we introduce "Adaptor," a framework designed to enhance LLM generalization by adapting them to specific tasks. Adaptor operates by first identifying a set of representative few-shot examples for a target task and then automatically selecting a subset of source tasks from the pre-trained LLM's knowledge base that are most similar. These tasks are then used to generate synthetic prompt data, which serves as the basis for fine-tuning the model. This approach effectively bridges the gap between the vast, diverse pre-training data and the specific requirements of the target task. Empirical results demonstrate that Adaptor significantly outperforms existing methods, achieving up to a 10% improvement in zero-shot generalization accuracy on the CLUTRR dataset.

We introduce the Mapillary Traffic Signal Dataset, a global collection of 3.5 million traffic signal images gathered from 100 countries. This resource is designed to support research on traffic signal detection and classification. To facilitate detection, we provide an online, publicly accessible map featuring annotated locations of all traffic signals. Furthermore, we have curated a subset of 10,000 images from 80 countries, which includes bounding box annotations for traffic signals and labels for signal light states. Our analysis evaluates the performance of various detection and classification models trained on this data.

Collaborative filtering (CF) has become a cornerstone of recommender systems, yet most existing methods depend on user-item interactions to train their models. This reliance on explicit feedback creates a significant challenge for recommender systems in cold-start scenarios, where users and items lack sufficient historical data. To address this limitation, we introduce SelfCF, a self-supervised collaborative filtering framework designed to learn robust representations for both users and items even in the absence of direct feedback. Our approach utilizes a novel self-supervised task that constructs a graph by linking users and items based on their shared neighbors. We then employ a graph neural network (GNN) to extract latent features from this graph, which are subsequently integrated into a CF model to generate personalized recommendations. Comprehensive experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate that SelfCF significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving improvements of up to 10.5% in Hit Ratio@10 for cold-start recommendations. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/ChenruiKilo/SelfCF.
